function.name: music_theory_primary_triads
function.description: Get the primary triads for a given key signature. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

message.content:
### The “core” of pop‑song harmony

In most contemporary pop songs the harmonic palette is **very diatonic** – it stays within the key and uses the seven triads that belong to that key.  
These triads are usually written with Roman numerals:

| Roman numeral | Function | Example in C major | Common pop‑song usage |
|---------------|----------|--------------------|-----------------------|
| **I**         | Tonic    | C                  | “Let It Be” (C)       |
| **ii**        | Super‑tonic | Dm              | “Someone Like You” (Dm) |
| **iii**       | Mediant  | Em                 | “Pachelbel’s Canon” (Em) |
| **IV**        | Subdominant | F              | “Happy Birthday” (F) |
| **V**         | Dominant | G                  | “All of Me” (G)       |
| **vi**        | Submediant | Am              | “Someone Like You” (Am) |
| **vii°**      | Leading‑tone | Bdim          | “Fly Me to the Moon” (Bdim) |

> **Why these chords?**  
> • They are diatonic, so they sound “in‑key” and resolve naturally.  
> • They cover the full range of tension/resolution that listeners expect.  
> • They’re easy to play on guitar, piano, and other instruments.

---

### The most common chord progressions

| Progression | Roman numerals | Typical feel | Pop‑song examples |
|-------------|----------------|--------------|-------------------|
| **I–V–vi–IV** | C–G–Am–F (in C) | Bright, anthemic | “Let It Be”, “With or Without You”, “No Woman No Cry” |
| **I–IV–V** | C–F–G | Classic, “happy” | “Happy Birthday”, “Twist and Shout” |
| **I–vi–IV–V** | C–Am–F–G | Pop‑ballad feel | “All of Me”, “Someone Like You” |
| **vi–IV–I–V** | Am–F–C–G | Emotional, “hook” | “Someone Like You”, “Apologize” |
| **ii–V–I** | Dm–G–C | Jazz‑influenced, smooth | “Fly Me to the Moon”, “Just the Way You Are” |
| **I–V–vi–iii–IV–I–IV–V** | C–G–Am–Em–F–C–F–G | Pachelbel‑style | “Pachelbel’s Canon” (used in many pop covers) |

> **Axis of Awesome** – the four‑chord cycle (I–V–vi–IV) is so ubiquitous that the band *Axis of Awesome* built a whole show around it.  
> **Pachelbel’s Canon** – the eight‑chord sequence (I–V–vi–iii–IV–I–IV–V) appears in countless pop songs, especially in ballads and cinematic pop.

---

### Quick reference: chords in a few keys

| Key | I | ii | iii | IV | V | vi | vii° |
|-----|---|----|-----|----|---|----|------|
| C   | C | Dm | Em  | F  | G | Am | Bdim |
| G   | G | Am | Bm  | C  | D | Em | F#dim |
| D   | D | Em | F#m | G  | A | Bm | C#dim |
| A   | A | Bm | C#m | D  | E | F#m| G#dim |

> **Tip:** If you’re playing guitar, the I–V–vi–IV progression in C (C–G–Am–F) becomes the classic “C–G–Am–F” shape, which is one of the first chord shapes most beginners learn.

---

### Bottom line

- **Diatonic triads** (I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi, vii°) form the backbone of pop harmony.  
- The **I–V–vi–IV** progression is the most ubiquitous “hook” in pop.  
- Other staples include **I–IV–V**, **I–vi–IV–V**, **vi–IV–I–V**, and the **ii–V–I** jazz‑influenced turn.  
- Many pop songs borrow the **Pachelbel Canon** sequence for a lush, cinematic feel.

These patterns give pop songs their familiar, sing‑along quality while keeping the harmony simple enough for both performers and listeners to grasp instantly.
